fluff.overview: The SOAR (Search-Over And Rescue) VTOL was developed by Yan Manufacturing on New Samarkand and introduced in 3018 under the direction of Luthien Armor Works. The design fills a niche role in civilian emergency services and light logistics, offering an affordable and mechanically simple airframe suited to search-and-rescue operations, medical evacuation, and passenger transport in difficult terrain. Though not a combat platform, the SOAR attracted attention beyond its intended market when security and paramilitary organizations recognized its quiet propulsion system and extended range as valuable assets. Its compact construction and fuel cell powerplant make it inexpensive to operate, and its open-architecture cargo bays support a variety of mission-specific equipment configurations.
fluff.capabilities:
The SOAR is powered by an electric fuel cell engine, giving it a especially quiet operational signature compared to conventional combustion or fusion-powered airframes. This low acoustic profile is one of the design's most prized features and a key factor in its adoption by paramilitary users. The airframe uses pre-molded pocket compartments along the fuselage to accommodate extra fuel cells, extending effective range to nearly 1,000 kilometers, a substantial improvement over most civilian-tier VTOLs.

The vehicle can seat up to six passengers or paramedics and is equipped with a myomer tether assembly along the doorframe, allowing vertical pickups without a prepared landing zone. Active vibration control works in concert with the rotors to further reduce noise output. The SOAR cruises at a moderate pace and can sustain over 100 kilometers per hour for extended periods without straining the powerplant.

The design's weaknesses are closely tied to its civilian mandate. Armor protection is minimal, and any sustained hostile fire poses a serious threat. The SOAR carries no weapon systems. It is entirely dependent on escort or distance from threat for survivability in contested environments, and its open-bay configuration offers no protection to passengers against weapons effects.
fluff.deployment: The SOAR sees its heaviest use in civilian emergency services, with search-and-rescue teams, medical evacuation units, and mountain rescue organizations operating it throughout the Draconis Combine and beyond. The Free Rasalhague Republic and Lyran Alliance both field significant numbers. In paramilitary roles, select ISF DEST teams employ the SOAR as an air cover and insertion support asset, relying on its low acoustic signature and extended range for operations where a louder or larger airframe would compromise mission security.
fluff.history:
Kenneth and Bella Yan established Yan Manufacturing in 3009 on New Samarkand, drawing on Kenneth's decades of experience as a firefighter with the New Samarkand Fire Department. The couple had long been enthusiasts of personal aviation, and they entered the chopper kit market with designs derived from the Wakazashi Airframe Ruckus-class acrobatic helicopter. Sales were modest in the early years, and the company nearly folded before an unexpected moment of publicity changed its trajectory.

During the 3013 Galedon Acrobatic Tour, pilot Michael Hulis scored a near-perfect 97.23 using a Yan Stutter-class single-seat chopper, drawing widespread attention to the small firm. Demand surged in the aftermath, and the Yans expanded their workforce and production capacity. Kenneth died in 3017, and Bella subsequently sold a controlling interest to Luthien Armor Works, stipulating that LAW retain the Yan name and continue producing compact VTOL airframes. LAW honored the arrangement and immediately tasked engineers with developing a dedicated utility design to compete with Wakazashi Airframe's AirRescue model.

The SOAR entered service in 3018 and proved popular across multiple markets. It spread quickly in the Free Rasalhague Republic and attracted interest from the Lyran Alliance, where mountain rescue units adopted it in significant numbers. The Royal Tharkad Mountain Patrol maintains at least six SOARs in regular rotation. Some ISF DEST teams also acquired the SOAR for insertion support, using its quiet propulsion and extended range to provide overhead cover during covert operations.
